questions.question: What is the total number of squares of all sizes in a 3x3 grid of unit squares?
What is the total number of squares of all sizes in a 4x4 grid of unit squares?
What is the general formula for the total number of squares (all sizes) in an n x n grid of unit squares?
questions.rationale: The total is the sum of squares 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2, which has the closed form n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.

questions.question: In a 2x3 rectangular grid (2 rows, 3 columns of unit squares), how many 1x1 squares are there?
questions.rationale: A 2-row by 3-column grid of unit cells contains 2 x 3 = 6 unit squares.

questions.question: What is the key difference between counting 'squares' and counting 'rectangles' in a grid?
options: They are exactly the same count
Squares require equal width and height, while rectangles allow any width-height combination, so every square is a rectangle but not vice versa
Rectangles are always larger than squares
Squares can only appear in odd-sized grids
questions.rationale: A square is a special case of a rectangle with equal width and height — so counting rectangles includes all squares plus every non-square rectangle.

questions.question: What is the formula for counting the total number of rectangles (including squares) in a grid with 'a' vertical boundary lines and 'b' horizontal boundary lines?
options: a x b
questions.rationale: Any rectangle is uniquely determined by choosing 2 of the 'a' vertical lines and 2 of the 'b' horizontal lines as its sides, giving C(a,2) x C(b,2).

questions.question: Why does counting rectangles by choosing boundary lines work as a method?
options: It doesn't actually work reliably
Because any rectangle is uniquely determined by choosing 2 vertical lines and 2 horizontal lines from the grid as its sides
Because it only counts the largest rectangle
Because it ignores squares entirely
questions.rationale: Every valid rectangle corresponds to exactly one choice of 2 vertical and 2 horizontal grid lines as its four sides, making this a reliable one-to-one counting method.

questions.question: In a grid with 4 vertical lines and 3 horizontal lines, how many total rectangles can be formed?
questions.rationale: C(4,2) x C(3,2) = 6 x 3 = 18 total rectangles.

questions.question: What is a 'basic triangle' in this lesson's terminology?
options: The largest triangle in the figure
The smallest, undivided triangular region in a figure, not made up of smaller sub-triangles
Any triangle with a right angle
A triangle formed only by diagonals
questions.rationale: A basic triangle is the smallest, undivided triangular region — the fundamental building block that composite (larger) triangles are formed from.

questions.question: Why do grid formulas (like the squares formula) work reliably across different grid sizes?
options: They only work for one specific grid size
Because they systematically count every valid position and size of a shape based on the grid's fixed structure, rather than relying on case-by-case visual counting
Because grids never actually vary in size
Because they ignore the grid's boundary lines
questions.rationale: Grid formulas are derived from the grid's consistent structure, so they systematically account for every valid size and position of a shape regardless of how large the grid is.
